title: "All are welcome" sampler in cross-stitch
subtitle: A bordered sampler with the phrase and small pride motifs on 14-count Aida
excerpt: "All are welcome" is a 120-by-100 stitch bordered sampler on 14-count Aida. The phrase sits in a large block alphabet at the centre; a rainbow flag stripe border frames the piece; and four small corner motifs (a heart, a star, a hand, and an arrow) fill the corners. Twelve floss colours. Finished size is about 21 x 18 cm.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library.

content.text: "All are welcome" is a 120-by-100 stitch bordered sampler on 14-count
. The phrase runs in a 9-stitch-tall uppercase alphabet at the centre of the piece, with each word on a separate row. A rainbow stripe
border, six colours in parallel rows, frames the whole piece. Four small full-cross motifs (one in each corner) anchor the layout. Twelve
colours. The INTERMEDIATE rating reflects the number of elements and the border planning rather than any difficult technique.

items.name: 14-count Aida, white
items.substitutions: White is best here, the rainbow border reads brightest against white

items.name: DMC floss for rainbow border
items.substitutions: Same rainbow colours as the coming-out hoop

items.name: DMC floss for corner motifs
items.qty: 1 skein each: 321 (heart/red), 3325 (blue for arrow/star), 3820 (yellow for hand)

items.name: Rectangular frame
items.substitutions: A large hoop works for stitching but the piece suits a frame for display

content.text: Plan the letter layout before stitching. Count the width of each row across two lines and check that the widest row fits inside the border.
Stitch the four corner motifs first to anchor the inner border corners. Then work the rainbow stripe border from each corner toward the centre of each side.
Stitch the text from the centre letter of the widest row outward. Work "ALL" above in a second pass.
Add the back-stitch border lines in the rainbow stripe colours after all full-cross work is complete. Each stripe is a single row of back-stitch in the corresponding rainbow colour.

Wash gently and press face-down until the stitches sit smooth and flat. A white mount and light natural wood frame suit the piece. This is a display piece for a hallway, door area, or community space.

items.symptom: The border letters are a different size from the centre text
items.cause: The border font uses a different stitch count per letter than the main text font.
items.fix: The border uses a 5-stitch-tall font; the main text uses 7 stitches. Count the chart carefully before switching between the two zones. Once the stitch counts are confirmed for each zone, start with the border and work inward to the main text.

items.symptom: The rainbow flag bar at the base looks uneven
items.cause: Each flag stripe was stitched in one long pass rather than in short sections checked against the chart width.
items.fix: Count the full width of the flag bar on the chart first. Stitch each stripe as a complete horizontal band and check the left and right edges align before starting the next colour. Once all stripes are in, the bar edges should be straight and even across the width.

content.text: For a larger piece with more corner motifs and a wider border, try the family name banner or house name sampler. Both are in the quotes-and-sayings sub-category and can be stitched in pride palette colours.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.
